analysis.one_liner: Extends overtime pay and full wage protections to farm workers, phasing down the overtime threshold to 40 hours.
analysis.headline: The Fairness for Farm Workers Act was introduced in July 2023 and referred to the Senate labor committee, which never acted on it; the bill died without a single vote when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: Farm workers are currently excluded from many of the wage rules other workers get under the Fair Labor Standards Act: they can be required to work long hours with no overtime pay, and certain farm jobs are exempt from minimum wage and overtime rules entirely. This bill removes those exclusions. It phases in an overtime requirement starting at 55 hours a week in 2024 and stepping down to 40 hours by 2027 (2030 for farms with 25 or fewer employees), and it wipes out the list of narrow agricultural exemptions from minimum wage and overtime protections. The bill never got a hearing, a markup, or a vote in either chamber.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly two million farm workers in the United States, who today can be worked 60 or more hours a week with no overtime premium and, in several narrow job categories, with no guaranteed minimum wage. Under the bill they would earn time-and-a-half past the weekly threshold, phased to 40 hours by 2027 — or 2030 if they work for a farm with 25 or fewer employees.

how_it_helps.text: Phases in overtime pay for agricultural workers, starting at 55 hours a week in 2024, dropping to 50 in 2025, 45 in 2026, and 40 hours from 2027 on; farms with 25 or fewer employees get until 2030 to reach 40 hours.
Repeals the FLSA provision that exempts agriculture from overtime requirements altogether, so farm workers are treated like other covered workers.

Strikes a list of agricultural exemptions (sections 13(b)(12) through (16)) and narrows the small-farm exemption so that only employers whose employees are immediate family members, or truly tiny operations under the 500 man-days test, remain outside coverage.

analysis.who_pays: Farm employers, who would pay time-and-a-half for hours above the weekly threshold, with the cost highest for large operations and labor-intensive crops. Some of the cost could reach consumers through higher food prices, and some workers could see their scheduled hours cut to keep them under the threshold.

drawbacks.text: The overtime mandate raises growers' labor costs substantially, and growers warned that would mean reduced hours for workers, more mechanization, or higher food prices; some workers who want long hours during harvest could end up earning less overall.

The bill treats small farms more gently but still eventually subjects them to the same 40-hour threshold by 2030, which operators of small farms argue is a heavy compliance burden for businesses with thin margins.
The phase-in takes years: large employers do not reach the standard 40-hour threshold until 2027, and small employers not until 2030, so the full benefit arrives slowly.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For farm workers, the benefit is concrete: time-and-a-half for long weeks, on jobs where 60-hour weeks are common and overtime today does not exist. The honest cost is that growers face a real payroll increase, which would land partly on farm owners and partly on consumers through food prices, and could trim some workers' hours during peak season. The long phase-in and the extra four-year delay for small farms soften the shock to employers but also delay the benefit to workers. The main problem with the bill is not its design but its fate: it never received so much as a committee hearing, so no version of this tradeoff was ever debated on the record.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee on the day it was introduced, and no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever happened before Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Alex Padilla introduced the bill on July 12, 2023, joined by 12 other Democratic senators at introduction.

The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions, where it stayed for the remainder of the 118th Congress with no further action recorded.

The bill would have phased in an agricultural overtime threshold falling from 55 hours a week to 40 hours by 2027 (2030 for employers with 25 or fewer employees), and repealed the overtime exemption for agriculture.

The bill would also have removed a list of agricultural minimum wage and overtime exemptions and narrowed the small-farm exemption to immediate-family employees and operations using 500 or fewer man-days of labor.
Thirteen of 48 Senate Democrats and one of four Senate Independents cosponsored the bill; no Senate Republican did, and the bill never reached the floor or a committee vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Farm employers, who keep the current exemption that lets them avoid paying overtime to agricultural workers, are better off because the bill never moved. Workers on farms remain outside the overtime and wage protections other covered workers have.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Farm employers who avoid overtime costs

for.name: Sen. Alex Padilla
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Fairness for Farm Workers Act and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

for.name: 13 of 48 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; none of the chamber's 49 Republicans did.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on July 12, 2023 and took no recorded action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Senate leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for a vote at any point in the 118th Congress.

against.name: Farm industry groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed phasing in overtime pay for agricultural workers, arguing it would sharply raise labor costs for growers.

sides.party_line_note: All 15 cosponsors were Democrats or the chamber's Independent; no Republican cosponsor ever joined, and the bill stayed in a committee without action rather than coming to a vote.

industries.note: The bill removes the overtime and wage exemptions growers currently rely on, adding time-and-a-half pay above the weekly threshold. Their interest in keeping the exemption runs against the wage protections farm workers would gain.

industries.industry: Agricultural labor contractors and crew leaders
industries.note: The bill strikes exemptions covering several agricultural job categories, extending minimum wage and overtime rules to contractors who now operate outside them.
Some of growers' higher labor costs would likely pass through to food prices, though the phase-in spreads this over years.
